meta.title: The Cafe | Latte with Lata
meta.description: A neighbourhood cafe in Harrowfield with microphones on the corner table. Coffee from two streets over, breakfast done properly, a room built for talking.

hero.title: A ROOM BUILT FOR TALKING
hero.intro: Good coffee, a kitchen that takes breakfast seriously, and music quiet enough to talk over. 27 Bellwood Street, Harrowfield.
hero.alt: The cafe room in daylight: wooden tables, a long bench under the window and the counter at the back.

sections.title: FROM FIRST POUR TO LAST WORD
paragraphs: Lata Singh opened the doors in the spring of 2024 with a second-hand espresso machine, a borrowed oven and one rule: the music stays quiet enough to talk over.

The talking turned out to be the point. By autumn there were microphones on the corner table, and the people she had spent a career alongside, in clinics, councils and charities, started coming in to say what they could not say at a podium.

The microphones were not part of the plan. One Thursday a friend who runs a food bank stayed past closing to talk through a decision she could not raise at her own board table. Lata borrowed a recorder so they would remember what was said. The week after, someone at the next table asked if they could listen in.
So the chairs were turned to face the corner. Two second-hand microphones arrived in a shoebox, then a small mixer, then a lamp. Nobody has asked for the corner table back.

It is still a cafe first. Most of the week the corner table is just a table, and the most important thing we make is breakfast. On Thursday nights it is where someone with a hard job says what it actually took.
The machine has since been replaced. The rule has not.

sections.title: WHAT WE CARE ABOUT
sections.intro: Four things. None of them are complicated. All of them cost a little more than the alternative.

items.title: Coffee from two streets over
items.body: Our beans come from a small roaster two streets away. We buy what they are roasting that week, so the filter coffee changes with it. It is fresh, the supply line is a short walk, and there is someone to talk to when a bag is not right.

items.title: A kitchen that does breakfast properly
items.body: Eggs cooked to order. Croissants baked at six. Porridge that was started before you woke up. The kitchen is small, so the menu is short. We would rather do a dozen things well than thirty things quickly.

items.title: A room built for talking
items.body: No speakers over the tables. Soft surfaces, quiet music and chairs you can sit in for an hour. If you cannot hear the person across from you, we have done something wrong.

items.title: A living wage for the team
items.body: Everyone who works here is paid at least the local living wage, and tips are shared evenly across the shift. It adds a little to the price of a cup. We think that is the right price.

sections.placeholderNote: Roaster, in-house baking, living-wage and tip-sharing claims are placeholders. Confirm each with the client before launch.

sections.title: SEATS ABOUT FORTY
paragraphs: The room seats about 40. There is a long bench under the window, a dozen small tables, four stools at the counter and a few tables outside under the awning.
The corner table is the one with the microphones. Most of the week it is the best seat in the house for two people and a long conversation. On Thursday nights the other chairs turn to face it.
Order at the counter and find a seat. We bring everything to you.

sections.title: QUESTIONS PEOPLE ASK

items.q: Can I work here on a laptop?
items.a: Yes, on weekdays. The wifi is free and there are sockets along the window bench. At weekends between 10:00 am and 2:00 pm we ask you to keep laptops closed so the tables can turn.
Dogs are welcome at the outside tables, and there is a water bowl by the door. Inside, assistance dogs only.

items.q: Is there room for a pram?
items.a: Yes. The entry is step-free and there is space to park a pram by the window bench. We have high chairs and a changing table. When the room is full we may ask you to fold it.
No. We always keep some tables for walk-ins. If you want to be sure, book online. We hold a table for 15 minutes and sittings are 90 minutes. For more than 8 people, call or email us.

Tell us when you order. The menu marks vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and dairy-free dishes and anything that contains nuts, and the kitchen will talk you through any plate. It is one small kitchen that handles nuts, gluten, dairy and eggs, so we cannot promise a dish is free of traces.
Yes. The room is available on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday evenings from 6:30 pm, for up to 40 seated. Write to us with your date and numbers and we will reply within 2 working days.

sections.title: BEFORE YOU ORDER

items.title: Allergens
items.body: Tell us about any allergy when you order, every time. One small kitchen handles nuts, gluten, dairy, eggs, sesame and fish, so we cannot promise that any dish is free of traces. GF means made with gluten-free ingredients, not made in a gluten-free kitchen.

items.title: Where it comes from
items.body: Coffee from a roaster two streets over. Bread, croissants and cakes baked here each morning. Eggs are free range. Vegetables come from the Saturday market when the season allows.

items.title: Prices at the counter
items.body: The prices are for a cup at the counter. A seat by the window, or at the corner table, costs the same. Prices include tax. There is no service charge, and tips are shared evenly across the team.

items.title: Large groups
items.body: We can seat up to 8 on one booking. For a bigger group, call or email us a few days ahead and we will plan the tables and, if you like, a set menu.

hero.title: PULL UP A CHAIR
hero.intro: Coffee. Leadership. Purpose. Real conversation. A new episode every Thursday, recorded live at the corner table.
hero.alt: Two microphones on a cafe table with coffee cups, the room softly lit behind them.

sections.title: THERE'S MORE BEHIND EVERY MISSION
sections.lead: Thoughtful conversations with people building careers, organizations, and movements around purpose.
paragraphs: Latte with Lata is a conversational podcast with mission-driven leaders: people who have built careers, organizations or movements around purpose rather than profit alone. It has the warmth and pace of a conversation over coffee, and the substance of a real discussion about leadership, impact and the decisions that shape the work.

Most leadership shows are about scale, growth and metrics. This one is about the person behind the mission: their motivations, their doubts, and the human decisions behind the work. Real leadership lessons come out over coffee, not in a boardroom.
Behind every organization, movement, and meaningful career are difficult decisions, unexpected lessons, doubts, and defining moments. Latte with Lata brings those stories to the table.
sections.kicker: Pull up a chair and discover the stories behind mission-driven work.

sections.title: FOR PEOPLE BUILDING WITH PURPOSE
sections.lead: For leaders, aspiring leaders, professionals, and anyone searching for more meaning in the work they do.
items: Current and aspiring leaders in nonprofit, healthcare, public sector and social-impact organizations.
Professionals working out a career shift toward more purpose-driven work.
Listeners who prefer a long, honest conversation to polished expert content.
People who like leadership content but are tired of growth hacks and hustle.
sections.kicker: Latte with Lata is a space for conversations about leadership, impact, purpose, and the realities of mission-driven work.

sections.title: THE SAME FOUR PARTS, EVERY WEEK
sections.intro: Every conversation moves through the same four parts. Guests know them in advance. They do not get the questions.

items.title: The Origin Story
items.short: What actually pulled this leader into mission-driven work.
items.body: We start with what actually pulled the guest into this work, which is rarely the version in the annual report. It is usually a person, a phone call or a bad week.

items.title: The Hard Trade-off
items.short: A real decision where mission and practicality were in tension.
items.body: One real decision where the mission and the practical answer pulled in different directions. We ask what it cost, who disagreed, and whether they would make the same call again.

items.title: What No One Tells You
items.short: An honest, unpolished lesson from the work.
items.body: The honest, unpolished lesson: the thing the guest wishes someone had said in year one. No frameworks, just what happened and what they do differently now.

items.title: The Coffee Break
items.body: We finish lighter. What they are reading, how they take their coffee, and what they do when they are not doing this.

sections.note: Every episode has all four parts. The tag marks the part the conversation leaned on most.

sections.title: HOW AN EPISODE WORKS
sections.intro: Every episode is recorded live in the cafe, in front of whoever turns up. There is no studio and no second take.

steps.title: Doors
steps.body: The cafe reopens and the chairs turn to face the corner table. It is free. Seats are first come, first seated, or you can reserve one.

steps.title: Recording
steps.body: One guest, one conversation, four parts, with a short break halfway. We finish by 8:15 pm. No slides, no panel, no pitch.

steps.title: The guest stays for a coffee
steps.body: There is no question time on the recording. The guest stays in the room afterwards, so ask them in person.

steps.title: The episode comes out
steps.body: We cut the evening down to about 45 minutes. The coughs come out and the pauses stay in. It is on every platform the following Thursday morning.

sections.title: MEET LATA
sections.name: Lata Singh

image.alt: Lata Singh, host of Latte with Lata.

paragraphs: Lata Singh hosts Latte with Lata. She comes to these conversations as a practitioner, not as an outside observer.

By day she is a senior operating leader in one of the country's largest safety-net healthcare networks, overseeing operations, quality, workforce and finance at scale. That work has given her hands-on fluency in what mission-driven organizations deal with every day: compliance, funding structures, workforce and public accountability.
She is also pursuing doctoral study in leadership and innovation, which brings an academic and reflective lens to the table alongside the operational one.
That is the edge of the show. She is fluent in the pressures, the trade-offs and the quiet victories that come with running a purpose-built organization, and those are the things she asks about.
credentials: Senior operating leader in one of the country's largest safety-net healthcare networks: operations, quality, workforce and finance at scale.
Hands-on fluency in compliance, funding structures, workforce and public accountability.

pullQuote.text: The most honest things leaders have told me were said over coffee, after the meeting, with nothing left to prove. I want that conversation, with the microphone switched on.

sections.title: BE A GUEST, OR SUGGEST ONE
paragraphs: We look for people who run something built around a mission: a clinic, a council service, a charity, a school, a social enterprise. Job title matters less than whether you have a decision you are willing to talk about honestly.
You do not need media training or a book to promote. You need an evening, an origin story and one hard trade-off.

The decision or lesson you think is worth an hour.
Thursdays you could be in Harrowfield.

meta.title: Episodes | Latte with Lata
meta.description: Every recent episode of Latte with Lata: mission-driven leaders on origin stories, hard trade-offs and what no one tells you. New every Thursday.

hero.title: THE CONVERSATIONS
hero.intro: Eighty-eight Thursdays so far. Here are the most recent, with notes on what each guest was willing to say out loud.
hero.alt: Headphones and a cup of coffee beside a notebook on a wooden cafe table.

items.title: The grant we turned down
items.blurb: Marisol said no to the biggest cheque in her nonprofit's history. On strings, dignity, and the board meeting that followed.
notes: Why the largest grant on offer came with terms that would have changed who the food bank could serve.
How she took the decision to her board, and what the vote looked like.
What she now tells other directors: read the conditions before you read the amount.
items.quote: The cheque was real. So were the strings. I had to decide which one we could live with.
items.coverAlt: Cover image for episode 88: The grant we turned down.

items.title: What no one tells you about a waiting room
items.blurb: Kwame runs a clinic where nobody is turned away. On the maths of a Tuesday morning, and the lesson no residency teaches.
notes: The arithmetic of a walk-in clinic: forty chairs, two doctors and a Tuesday morning.
Why he stopped judging a day by how fast the room empties.
The lesson no residency teaches: people need to feel they were right to come.
items.quote: Nobody trains you for the waiting room. It is where most of the care actually happens.
items.coverAlt: Cover image for episode 87: What no one tells you about a waiting room.

items.title: Fixing a form nobody could finish
items.blurb: Hannah rebuilt a benefits form that failed half the people who started it. On slow change inside government, and who decides it worked.
notes: A benefits form that half of all applicants gave up on, and how her team found out where.
Trading a fast relaunch for six months of testing with the people who fill it in.
Who gets to say a public service worked: the department, the auditor or the applicant.
items.quote: We asked people to prove they were struggling in forty-one questions. We got it down to twelve.
items.coverAlt: Cover image for episode 86: Fixing a form nobody could finish.

items.title: The origin story is not the pitch
items.blurb: Elias hires people on the day they leave prison. On the phone call that started it, a first year of losses, and keeping the door open.
notes: The phone call from a former colleague that started Second Shift.
A first year of losses, and the month he nearly closed the doors.
Why he hires on release day, before anyone has a reference.
items.quote: The pitch says we had a vision. The truth is a man called me and needed a job by Monday.
items.coverAlt: Cover image for episode 85: The origin story is not the pitch.

items.title: Showing up is the whole strategy
items.blurb: Rosa has knocked on more doors than she can count. On patience, small wins, and what a street knows that a strategy deck does not.
notes: What knocking on doors teaches you that a survey never will.
Why small wins, like a fixed stairwell light, build a union faster than big demands.
How she handles burnout, her own and other people's.
items.quote: A street knows things no strategy deck will tell you. You just have to keep turning up.
items.coverAlt: Cover image for episode 84: Showing up is the whole strategy.

items.title: Who stays when everyone is leaving
items.role: Director of nursing, St Oswin's Hospice
items.blurb: Grace kept a hospice team together through the hardest three years in nursing. On staying, and the coffee break that saved a shift.
notes: How she kept a hospice team together while nurses were leaving the profession.
The ten-minute coffee break she made compulsory, and what it did for a shift.
A lighter close: night-shift snacks, bad pens and the playlist in her car.
items.quote: I could not pay them more. I could make sure nobody ate lunch standing up.
items.coverAlt: Cover image for episode 83: Who stays when everyone is leaving.

items.title: The budget line nobody wanted to own
items.blurb: Tomasz had to choose between fixing roofs and keeping rents flat. On spreadsheets with people in them, and telling tenants the truth.
notes: Why a housing trust could not afford repairs and a rent freeze in the same year, and how he showed the board.
The tenant meeting where he put the real numbers on the wall.
What finance people owe the front line: plain words, early.
items.quote: Every line in that budget was somebody's kitchen ceiling. You cannot hide behind the word variance.
items.coverAlt: Condenser microphone on a desk with guitars hanging on the wall behind

items.title: I came for a summer job
items.blurb: Leilani took a summer job at a youth centre and never left. On being needed at nineteen, and learning to run the place at thirty.
notes: The summer job that was meant to last ten weeks.
What changed when she went from youth worker to the person who signs the payroll.
Why she still runs the Friday drop-in herself.
items.quote: I did not choose the sector. A fourteen-year-old asked if I was coming back on Monday, and I was.
items.coverAlt: Freshly roasted coffee beans turning in the cooling tray of a roaster

items.title: What no one tells you about a merger
items.role: Chief executive, Two Rivers Family Services
items.blurb: Anjali merged two charities that had competed for twenty years. On grief in the staff room, and the logo row that was never about a logo.
notes: Why two organizations with the same mission spent twenty years competing for the same grants.
The staff-room grief nobody put in the merger plan.
What she would do in the first ninety days if she did it again.
items.quote: Nobody warned me a merger is a bereavement. People were mourning a letterhead, and they were right to.
items.coverAlt: Wooden folding bistro chairs and a table on the pavement against a terracotta-red wall

items.title: The night shift taught me to lead
items.blurb: Mateus spent eleven years on an ambulance before he ran the roster. On what 3 am teaches about calm, and why he still rides along.
notes: Eleven years on the road, and the call that made him apply for the office job.
Building a roster that treats sleep as a safety issue.
Why he still works one night shift a month.
items.quote: At 3 am nobody cares about your title. They care whether you are calm. I try to manage like that.
items.coverAlt: Cafe bar counter with a large lampshade and staff working behind it

items.title: Closing the programme that worked
items.role: Head of programmes, Open Book Literacy Trust
items.blurb: Naledi closed a reading programme with strong results and no funding. On ending things well, and telling forty volunteers the truth.
notes: How a programme can hit every target and still lose its funding.
The choice between stretching it thin and closing it properly.
How to tell forty volunteers, and what she handed over to the schools.
items.quote: It worked, and we still had to stop. Those two facts sat at the same table for a long time.
items.coverAlt: Three friends toasting with coffee cups above a wooden cafe table

items.title: Late fees, long walks and lending a book twice
items.blurb: Eleanor scrapped late fees and watched the books come back. A lighter one: walking to work, conference coffee, and what she lends twice.
notes: What happened to returns in the year after the library dropped late fees.
Her forty-minute walk to work, and why she will not give it up.
The three books she presses on people, and the one she stopped recommending.
items.quote: A library is the last place you can sit all day and nobody asks what you are buying.
items.coverAlt: Silver condenser microphone in a shock mount with a pop filter in a dark studio

items.title: Nobody trains you to be your friends' boss
items.blurb: Daniyal went from the staff room to the principal's office in one summer. On lonely lunches, hard reviews, and keeping friendships honest.
notes: Going from colleague to principal over one summer holiday.
The first performance review he had to give a friend.
Where a school leader finds peers when the staff room is no longer his.
items.quote: The day I got the job, the staff room went quiet when I walked in. Nobody tells you about that.
items.coverAlt: A small round table with flowers and two chairs in a bright corner next to an old upright piano

items.title: We said yes to the contract
items.blurb: Emiko took a public contract that doubled her shelter's beds and its paperwork. On what the money changed, and what she would sign again.
notes: Why she said yes to a contract her own staff were split on.
What reporting requirements did to the front desk, and how they fixed it.
The clause she would negotiate harder next time.
items.quote: We got forty more beds and four hundred more pages. I would still sign it. I would read it slower.
items.coverAlt: Barista in a flat cap and apron working at an espresso machine

items.title: My mother's kitchen table
items.blurb: Beatriz grew up translating letters for her neighbours. On turning a kitchen table into an advice centre, and the first case she lost.
notes: Translating official letters for neighbours at nine years old.
From a kitchen table to a registered advice centre with four staff.
The first case she lost, and what it changed about how she promises help.
items.quote: I was nine, reading a landlord's letter to a grown man. That was the first day of this job.
items.coverAlt: A cappuccino, a paperback and a pot of purple flowers on a small wooden table by a cushioned window bench

items.title: What no one tells you about public money
items.blurb: Farid hands out public money for a living and says the job is mostly listening. On audits, trust, and the application he still thinks about.
notes: What a grants manager actually does between the deadline and the decision.
Why audits are not the enemy, and when they are.
The application he turned down and still thinks about.
items.quote: Public money comes with a thousand rules and one question: could you explain this to a neighbour?
items.coverAlt: A studio condenser microphone in a shock mount against warm red tones

items.title: A choir, a van and a very old dog
items.blurb: Siobhan coordinates ninety volunteers and sings alto on Tuesdays. A lighter one: the delivery van, her old dog, and never saying busy.
notes: How she keeps ninety volunteers turning up, and why she learns every name.
The delivery van that has outlasted three coordinators.
Choir on Tuesdays, and why she has banned the word busy.
items.quote: Volunteers do not leave because of the work. They leave because nobody learned their name.
items.coverAlt: Cafe interior with a dark leather banquette, wooden tables and a copper pendant lamp

items.title: Starting again at fifty
items.role: Founder, Spoke and Chain Bike Workshop
items.blurb: Henry left a bank at fifty to teach teenagers to fix bikes. On a pay cut, a cold garage, and the first kid who came back to teach.
notes: Leaving a thirty-year banking career without a plan B.
The first winter in an unheated garage with six teenagers and four bikes.
What it meant when a former trainee came back as an instructor.
items.quote: I spent thirty years moving numbers. Now a kid rides off on something we fixed. I can see that.
items.coverAlt: Loaves, pastries and fruit slices piled on a bakery counter under black pendant lamps, staff blurred behind

sections.title: THE RECORDING NIGHT
sections.lead: Coffee. Leadership. Purpose. Real conversation. Thursday nights from 6:30 pm the chairs turn to face the corner table, and there is one for you.
paragraphs: Every episode of the podcast is recorded live in the cafe on a Thursday night, in front of whoever turns up. One guest, one conversation, four parts, with a short break halfway.
It is free. Seats are first come, first seated. If you want to be sure of a chair, reserve one online and we will hold it until 6:50 pm.
The kitchen runs a short list of plates until 8:30 pm and the counter stays open. When the recording ends the guest stays for a coffee, and so can you.

facts.label: Seats
facts.value: 40. First come, first seated, or reserve to be sure.

timeline.label: The cafe closes for half an hour while we turn the room.
Doors. Find a seat, order a drink, order a plate.
Reserved seats that are still empty go to the room.
Recording starts. Phones on silent. There is a short break halfway.
Recording ends. The guest stays for a coffee.
We lock up, give or take a conversation.

sections.title: WHAT WE DO WITH YOUR DETAILS
sections.reviewNote: Template for legal review. Written in plain language for the study build; it has not been checked by a lawyer and must be reviewed against local privacy law before launch.
sections.intro: This is a plain summary of what this site collects, why, and how long we keep it. We collect as little as we can.

blocks.title: Who we are
blocks.body: Latte with Lata, 27 Bellwood Street, Harrowfield. For anything about your data, email hello@lattewithlata.example or ask at the counter.

blocks.title: When you book a table or reserve a seat
blocks.body: We collect your name, email, phone number, the date, time and size of your party, and any occasion or notes you choose to add. We use them to hold your table, to contact you if something changes, and to recognise you if you book again. We keep booking records for 12 months after the date of the booking, then delete them.

blocks.title: When you send us a message
blocks.body: We collect your name, email, phone number if you give one, the topic and your message. We use them to reply. We keep messages for 12 months after our last reply, then delete them.

blocks.title: When you join the newsletter
blocks.body: We collect your email address, the date you agreed and the page you signed up on. We use it to send one email a week. We keep it until you unsubscribe, which you can do from any email or by asking us.

blocks.title: Marketing
blocks.body: We only send marketing email if you tick the box. Booking without ticking it changes nothing about your booking.

blocks.title: Who sees it
blocks.body: Cafe staff who need it to run bookings and answer messages. We do not sell your details, share them with advertisers or pass them to the host's employer or any other institution.

blocks.title: Cookies
blocks.body: The public site sets no advertising or tracking cookies. The staff sign-in to the booking system uses one essential cookie.

blocks.title: Recording nights
blocks.body: Thursday recordings are audio-recorded and sometimes photographed. We say so at the door. Tell a member of staff if you would rather stay out of photos.

blocks.title: Asking us to delete or correct something
blocks.body: Email hello@lattewithlata.example from the address you used, or ask at the counter. Tell us what you want removed: a booking, a message, your newsletter sign-up or everything. We confirm within 2 working days and finish within 30 days. We may need to keep anything the law requires us to keep.

sections.placeholderNote: Retention for messages (12 months), the 30-day completion time and the cookie statement are proposals. Only the 12-month booking retention comes from the brief.

success.emailLine: We have also sent these details to your email.
success.emailLineNote: Show emailLine only once confirmation emails are really sent. The study build writes to an outbox file and sends nothing.

sections.fallback: Online booking and messages are switched off on this copy of the site. Call (555) 014-2024 or email hello@lattewithlata.example and we will sort it out by hand.

items.title: We hold your table for 15 minutes
items.body: After that it goes back to the room. Call if you are running late and we will do what we can.

items.title: Sittings are 90 minutes
items.body: Long enough for breakfast and a second coffee. If nobody is waiting, stay as long as you like.

items.title: Parties over 8: call or email
items.body: We plan big tables by hand. Call (555) 014-2024 or email hello@lattewithlata.example a few days ahead.

items.title: Cancel up to 2 hours before
items.body: Use Manage a booking with your reference and email. Inside 2 hours, please call so the table can go to someone else.

items.title: No deposit, no card
items.body: Booking is free. Recording nights are free too.

sections.title: MANAGE A BOOKING
sections.intro: Enter your booking reference and the email you booked with.

reference.label: Booking reference
reference.help: Six characters after LWL-. It was shown when you booked.

cancel.confirmText: Your booking for {party} on {date} at {time} will be cancelled. This cannot be undone.
cancel.done: Booking {reference} is cancelled. Thank you for letting us know.
cancel.tooLate: It is less than 2 hours before your booking, so it cannot be cancelled online. Please call (555) 014-2024.
cancel.alreadyCancelled: This booking has already been cancelled.

sections.change: To change the day, time or party size, cancel this booking and make a new one, or call us and we will move it for you.

email.required: Enter the email you booked with.
email.invalid: That email does not look right. Check it and try again.

errors.not_found: We could not find a booking with that reference and email. Check both and try again.
errors.too_late: It is less than 2 hours before your booking, so it cannot be cancelled online. Please call (555) 014-2024.
errors.not_cancellable: This booking can no longer be cancelled online. Please call (555) 014-2024.
errors.already_cancelled: This booking has already been cancelled.
errors.server_error: Something went wrong on our side. Nothing was changed. Try again, or call (555) 014-2024.
errors.rate_limited: That is a lot of attempts in a short time. Wait a few minutes and try again.
errors.unavailable: The booking system is not answering right now. Try again in a minute, or call (555) 014-2024.
errors.network: You seem to be offline. Check your connection and try again.

sections.title: RATHER TALK TO A PERSON?
sections.text: Call (555) 014-2024 during opening hours, or write to us and we will reply within 2 working days.
